Relics
rĕl´ĭks
n. pl. (the bones, garments or possessions of a saint, kept and venerated as channels of grace)
Latin reliquiae, remains, from relinquere, to leave behind. Calvin's Treatise on Relics catalogued the trade and observed that the church had enough pieces of the true cross to freight a ship.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A relic is a physical remainder of a holy person kept for veneration. Scripture records two events the practice appeals to and neither establishes it: a dead man revived when he touched Elisha's bones (2Ki 13:21), a single unrepeated sign in a book of unrepeatable signs; and handkerchiefs from Paul's body healing the sick at Ephesus (Act 19:12), where the same chapter ends with the converts burning their magic books. Against the practice stands what Israel did with a genuine relic: Hezekiah “brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it” (2Ki 18:4). Moses' own grave was hidden, “but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day” (Deu 34:6). And at the empty tomb the question is, “Why seek ye the living among the dead?” (Luk 24:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines relics as the remains of the body of a saint; and, in a general sense, that which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest.

expand to see more

RELIC, n. That which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest; as the relics of a town; the relics of a former generation.

2. The body of a deceased person; remains.

3. In the Romish church, the remains of the body of a saint, or something which belonged to a saint, preserved with great veneration as sacred memorials.

Key Scripture

2Ki 13:21 — "And it came to pass, as they were burying a man, that, behold, they spied a band of men; and they cast the man into the sepulchre of Elisha: and when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet."

Act 19:12 — "So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them."

2Ki 18:4 — "He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan."

Deu 34:6 — "And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day."

Luk 24:5 — "And as they were afraid, and bowed down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the living among the dead?"

Modern Corruption

A genuine object of God's own giving became an object of worship within a few centuries, and Hezekiah's response to it is in the canon.

expand to see more

The brasen serpent is the whole argument. God commanded Moses to make it, healing came through it, and the Lord Himself used it as a figure of His own lifting up. Seven hundred years later Israel was burning incense to it, and a godly king broke it in pieces and gave it a contemptuous name — Nehushtan, a piece of brass. The object was authentic and the veneration was still idolatry. That single verse answers every defence of relics built on the genuineness of the article, because 2 Kings 18:4 concerns an article no one could dispute.

Deuteronomy 34:6 is the positive design. The Lord buried Moses Himself in a valley in Moab, and no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day — a deliberate concealment of the grave of the greatest prophet Israel had, by the God who knew exactly what would have been built over it. Jude adds the strange detail that Michael contended with the devil about that body. Where God has hidden a thing, the church's business is not to go looking for it.

The medieval trade was a commercial industry with pilgrimage revenue attached, and Calvin's catalogue is devastating precisely because it is dry: he simply lists the churches and counts the duplicate heads, arms and nails. But the deeper objection is not fraud, which would be answered by better provenance. It is that the living Christ has given His church a table, a font, a Book and His own Spirit, and a congregation drawn to a bone has been drawn away from all four. Why seek ye the living among the dead?

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew etsem (H6106), bone; nehushtan (H5180), a piece of brass; qeber (H6913), grave, sepulchre; Greek soudarion (G4676), handkerchief, napkin.

expand to see more

Hebrew etsem (H6106) — bone; 2 Kings 13:21, Genesis 2:23, Ezekiel 37:1–7.

Hebrew nehushtan (H5180) — Nehushtan, a thing of brass; 2 Kings 18:4 only — Hezekiah's contemptuous name for it.

Greek soudarion (G4676) — handkerchief, napkin; Acts 19:12, John 11:44, 20:7.

Usage

"“He brake in pieces the brasen serpent” — the article was genuine; the incense was not."

"“No man knoweth of his sepulchre” — God hid the grave, and knew why."

"“Why seek ye the living among the dead?” — asked at an empty tomb."
